summary: This informational RFC discusses how BGP-LS SPF applies in data centers built on Clos or Fat Tree topologies, giving simplified guidance for deploying it.

eli5.summary: It is a practical guide for using the BGP map-sharing trick in big data centers wired in tree-like layers.

subtitle: Deploying BGP link-state routing in data center Clos networks.

tldr.problem: Traditional BGP uses hop-by-hop routing and delays convergence in data centers, preventing the use of route reflectors and slowing reaction to network changes.
tldr.mechanism: BGP-LS-SPF extensions allow BGP to compute routes using link-state algorithms (like OSPF) instead of hop-by-hop decisions, giving every router a complete topology view.
tldr.outcome: Data centers using Clos or Fat Tree topologies can now deploy a single routing protocol that converges faster, allows centralized controllers, and simplifies operations.

today: RFC 9816 is an Informational specification providing guidance for deploying RFC 9815 (BGP-LS-SPF) in data center networks. It has not been obsoleted and represents the IETF consensus on practical deployment strategies for link-state BGP in Clos and Fat Tree topologies.

sections.title: BGP in Clos Topologies
sections.content:
Modern data centers build underlay networks using Clos topologies: a multi-stage network where every server can reach every other server via multiple equal-cost paths. Many data centers use BGP as a single routing protocol for simplicity, but traditional BGP is a path-vector protocol that decides routes hop-by-hop. Each router announces prefixes only after its own best-path computation, serializing convergence across the fabric and preventing the use of route reflectors (because EBGP sessions must match the data path).

The BGP-LS-SPF extensions add a new mode where BGP speakers use link-state algorithms (similar to OSPF) to compute routes instead of hop-by-hop decisions. This allows every router in the domain to learn the complete topology and calculate shortest paths independently, reducing convergence time and enabling new deployment models.
sections.eli5: Clos networks are wired like a tree with many paths. BGP-SPF lets all routers see the tree shape, so they all react to broken links instantly.

sections.title: Link-State Routing in BGP
sections.content:
BGP-SPF introduces the BGP-LS-SPF SAFI (Subsequent Address Family Identifier), which carries link-state Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) for nodes, links, and prefixes. Instead of the BGP best-path algorithm picking one route per prefix, BGP-SPF routers run SPF (Shortest Path First) to determine whether NLRI has changed and to compute routes. This separation means routing decisions are not serialized by best-path computations at intermediate hops.

BGP-SPF can coexist with standard BGP IP Unicast SAFI, allowing the same peering to carry both underlay link-state information and overlay VPN routes. The tiebreaking of route installation is a matter of local policy. Because BGP-SPF follows standard BGP procedures, all existing transport security mechanisms (TCP-MD5, BGPsec) are available.
sections.eli5: BGP-SPF sends out a map of all the links (like a GPS map) instead of just hop-by-hop directions. Routers all compute the best path from the same map.

sections.title: Deployment Models
sections.content:
BGP-SPF can be deployed in two ways: as full hop-by-hop peering (every link has a BGP session, converging faster than traditional BGP), or as sparse peering (only enough BGP sessions to form a biconnected graph, with BFD monitoring link availability). In sparse mode, Tier N-1 routers can act as route reflectors for Tier N.

One useful heuristic for sparse peering is the biconnected graph model: Top-of-Rack (ToR) switches use passive BGP session acceptance southbound (to servers), actively maintain two northbound sessions to different spine routers, and only establish east-west sessions if unable to reach two northbound peers. This pattern reduces peering overhead while maintaining topology redundancy.

Controllers (inside or outside the data path) can learn the topology directly from BGP-LS-SPF advertisements and compute traffic-engineered paths, eliminating the need for a separate topology protocol like OSPF or for controllers to query each router independently.
sections.eli5: Routers can talk just to neighbors they need instead of all neighbors, and controllers can ask any router for the full map.

sections.title: Policy and Simplifications
sections.content:
BGP policy (prefix filtering, AS path rules) can be applied at any level of the fabric. In Spine/Leaf topologies, leaf routers do not need to announce BGP-LS Prefix NLRI received from spines back to other spines; this can be enforced with a policy that filters NLRIs whose first AS is the spine AS.

For simplified peering in large data centers, BGP-SPF routers can use IPv6 link-local addresses and dynamic peer discovery (via IPv6 Router Advertisements or similar mechanisms) to avoid pre-configuring IPv4 addresses on every interface. The Link Local/Remote Identifiers of peering interfaces are used in the Link NLRI for biconnected graph validation.

Endpoints that wish to participate in the topology but never forward transit traffic (e.g., servers offering application services or controllers) can set the SPF Status TLV in their Node NLRI to exclude themselves from the SPF tree, ensuring no one routes through them.
sections.eli5: Routers can be told which announcements to repeat and which to keep quiet. IPv6 neighbors can discover each other automatically.

sections.title: Applicability and Benefits
sections.content:
BGP-SPF is most effective in Clos and Fat Tree topologies where dense meshes provide many equal-cost paths. In non-Clos topologies (like backbone networks), determining whether to establish a BGP session is more complex, though the convergence benefits still apply.

The key advantage is operational simplification: a single routing protocol (BGP) for both underlay and overlay, faster convergence due to link-state algorithms, and the ability to use controllers that learn the topology from the same advertisements used for routing. BGP-LS-SPF also works well with Data Center Interconnect (DCI) gateways, which typically have simpler connectivity and need not participate in the BGP-LS-SPF SAFI.

RFC 9816 is Informational and provides guidance for real-world data center deployments of the BGP-LS-SPF extensions defined in RFC 9815.
sections.eli5: One protocol handles everything, changes propagate instantly, and the system scales from small data centers to massive fabric.
